feature: A sound's volume line picks, shapes and answers right-click
summary: A right-click anywhere on a sound clip now opens its menu, the volume line included. The line follows the same rule as every animated line: a click picks a dot or the segment between two, only Command-click adds a dot, and a segment's right-click sets its curve (Ease out, Hold and the rest). The mix plays the bent line as drawn.
setup: Photonz Dev, release Next, no flag changed from its default. Open the sample recording and add the sample music (Add Sound) so it sits on Audio 2.

try.do: Pick the music, type 3 into Fades > In, then Command-click its volume line three times further along. Three dots appear and nothing you hear changes.
try.shotNote: Photographed with the window behind another app, the way a walk leaves it. Blue buttons and picked controls show their background look here; with the window in front they take the accent colour.

try.do: Click a dot, then click the line between two dots. Each click picks that one thing and adds nothing; Shift-click adds to the pick.
Right-click the fade's segment (the rise at the start) and choose Ease out.
try.shotNote: Photographed with the window behind another app, the way a walk leaves it. Blue buttons and picked controls show their background look here; with the window in front they take the accent colour.

try.do: Look at the picked segment: white on an accent edge, with a bend handle at its middle. Drag the handle up or down to bend it by hand. The panel's Fades section shows a Segment row with its curve.
try.shotNote: Photographed with the window behind another app, the way a walk leaves it. Blue buttons and picked controls show their background look here; with the window in front they take the accent colour.

try.do: Click a dot and press Backspace. The dot goes; Command-Z brings it back in one step.
Right-click the waveform, the line past the last dot, and the recording's own sound on the Audio track. Each opens the clip's menu.
try.shotNote: Photographed with the window behind another app, the way a walk leaves it. Blue buttons and picked controls show their background look here; with the window in front they take the accent colour.

try.do: Drag the line up or down away from the dots and the bend handle: it is still the fader for the whole clip.

evaluate: Can you now pick the dot or the segment you mean on the first try, without adding stray dots?
Is one bend handle at a segment's middle enough to shape a fade or a dip, or do you want the two handles the value graph shows?
Does a right-click on a segment lead with the right rows, with the clip's own rows underneath where you expect them?
Does the eased fade sound the way the line looks when you play it?
rough: This Mac's walks could not bring the probe to the front, so plain clicks never reached it. The plain-click rules (a click picks a dot or a segment, a single or double click never adds) are proven by unit tests and by a-sound-s-volume-line-plain-clicks-walk, which takes the front and comes round in the whole set. Command-click, right-click and Backspace were checked here for real.
A picked dot is white on an accent ring, where video-audio.html draws an active dot larger in its warning colour: settled by your rule on 2026-10-13 ("a selected thing should turn white").

A picked segment shows one bend handle at its middle (an even bend through the hand), not the two Bezier handles the value graph shows. A level line has no key handles to hang them from, and two handles next to a dot fight it for the click. Evaluate line 2 asks whether one is enough.
Right-click no longer moves the playhead anywhere on the timeline (your later rule on 2026-10-13); the task's older wording asked for it to move.

The task asked for a walk that double-clicks to add two dots; your later rule says only Command-click adds and a double click does nothing special, so the walks Command-click and check that a double click adds nothing.
Dragging a dot and the bend handle by hand were not driven by a walk on this Mac (the probe could not take the front for a drag); both write one undo step through the same code the menu uses.
